stories.headline: After hot CPI, a December hike is near-certain and a 50bp move is in play, with Waller leading the case
stories.dek: The Fed held at 3.75%–4.00% on Oct. 28 with two dissents for a hike; Tuesday's 0.3% core print hit the marker Governor Waller set for a bigger move.
tldr: Waller said a 50bp December hike should be considered if October core CPI hit 0.3%; core came in at **0.3%** (about 0.297% unrounded).
A **25bp** December hike is now seen as close to certain in some estimates (about 100%, from 84%); odds of **50bp** run roughly **10%–14%** depending on the source.
Chair Kevin Warsh has kept his communication guarded; the minutes on Nov. 18 and the Dec. 8–9 meeting are the next tests.
whatHappened: The Fed held its target range at 3.75%–4.00% on Oct. 28 with two officials [[dissenting|dissent]] in favor of a hike. Governor Christopher Waller had since said that a 0.3% or higher core CPI in October would justify considering a 50bp hike in December, while backing at least 25bp regardless. Tuesday's core CPI printed 0.3% (about 0.297% unrounded), and market estimates for a December hike of at least 25bp rose to near-certain in some measures, with 50bp odds at roughly 10% to 14%. Chair Warsh has not signaled a bigger move, and the sources I found differ on exact odds, so treat them as a range.
background: The Fed hiked in September after months of energy-driven inflation, and it is trying to avoid a repeat of the 1970s, when inflation expectations became unanchored. Warsh's style is to guard his communication, so markets read the dissents and the data rather than any explicit signal.
whyItMatters: The path matters for the front end of the curve and the dollar. Falling oil reduces the inflation argument for a hike, but a hot labor market and sticky core inflation keep it alive. A deeper equity selloff would add a growth argument against tightening.

grandLine.title: Kizaru's Unclear Justice
grandLine.body: Kizaru is the admiral whose intentions you can never quite read; his 'Unclear Justice' leaves everyone guessing what he'll do. A chair who keeps a hike 'in play' without saying yes or no creates the same effect: markets have to read each data point for the heading.

views.thesis: Inflation is still too hot to stop at 4%.
views.argument: Energy prices are feeding into core inflation, and the two dissenters wanted to act in October, so a December hike finishes the job.

views.thesis: Oil's drop and market stress argue for holding.
views.argument: Brent has fallen from the $115 area to the mid-$90s, equities are in a correction, and payroll growth is slow, so tightening risks over-tightening into a supply shock.

interview.question: Would you bet on a December hike?
interview.answer: I'd treat it as roughly a coin flip tilted toward a hike, and lean on the data. The Fed has dissenters wanting to tighten, but oil has fallen and equities are under stress. A [[hawkish hold|hawkish hold]] is the base case if payrolls are soft and oil stays lower. What changes my mind is a hot wage print or a re-spike in oil.

followUp.question: What's a hawkish hold?
followUp.answer: A decision to keep rates unchanged while signaling that hikes remain possible.

keyTerms.definition: Leaving rates unchanged while signaling that tightening is still a live option.
A formal vote against the committee's decision. Dissents hint at where the committee could move next.
keyTerms.example: Two officials dissented in favor of a hike on Oct. 28.

stories.headline: Iran's security chief denies talks with the US as Qatar reports progress and Washington extends its blockade
stories.dek: Mohsen Rezaei says Hormuz stays shut until seven conditions are met; Rubio says the sides aren't close to a breakthrough.
tldr: Iran's Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran is holding **no negotiations** with the US and Hormuz stays closed until **seven conditions** are met.
Rubio said the US is not close to a breakthrough and called Iran's demands outrageous; Qatar says it sees progress.
The US is pushing a military task force to extend its naval blockade; Iran's military dismissed it as 'wordplay.'
whatHappened: Iran's Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of the Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran is holding no negotiations with the United States and that Hormuz stays closed until Washington meets all seven of Iran's conditions. A separate report says Iran's proposal would resume talks within two days if the US halted attacks, lifted its blockade of Iranian ports and waived some sanctions. Secretary of State Rubio said the sides are not close to a breakthrough, citing outrageous Iranian demands, while Qatar, the main [[mediator|mediation]], said it saw progress after a White House meeting and Trump held a call with Qatar's emir.

Trump has said renewed strikes on Iran are 'highly unlikely' if Tehran agrees to a very strong nuclear deal and fully reopens Hormuz. The US is also pushing a military task force to extend its naval blockade, which Iran's military dismissed as 'wordplay.' CNN's Nov. 8 explainer describes quiet negotiations in which neither side has budged. No agreement has been announced.
background: The war began on Feb. 28 with US and Israeli strikes. A June memorandum and ceasefire collapsed in July, and Iran has since restricted shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Mediation has run on and off since, usually in parallel with strikes and threats, and traders call a peace-talk hope that fades a [[false dawn]].
whyItMatters: For readers following the world rather than the tape: this is the story that decides whether the Gulf stays at war. For markets it is the main driver of oil, which fell about 8% on Wednesday on hopes of an exit.

grandLine.title: Bounty posters vs. an Admiral
grandLine.body: The World Government warns with bounty posters first and only sends an Admiral if the warnings are ignored. 'No rush' on strikes is the poster stage: the threat is still on the wall, but the fleet hasn't sailed. Whether it ever does depends on whether the talks give Washington a face-saving exit.

views.thesis: Domestic politics and talks are pushing toward a deal.
views.argument: After the midterms rebuke, the administration has reasons to avoid a wider war, and Tehran is signaling flexibility by empowering its negotiators.
Israel's government reportedly wants a strike, Iranian officials say a deal is distant, and previous 'false dawns' ended in renewed fighting.

interview.question: What's the state of the US–Iran war?
interview.answer: A stalemate with talks running alongside a standoff. Qatar is mediating, Iran says its leader has backed the negotiators, and Trump is saying 'no rush' on strikes. But the sides remain far apart, and past pauses have collapsed. I'd watch Hormuz flows and whether a draft agreement emerges. What changes my mind is a signed memorandum or a new round of strikes.

followUp.question: Why does Qatar mediate?
followUp.answer: It has working channels to both Washington and Tehran and is a Gulf state with a stake in ending the conflict.

keyTerms.definition: A third party carrying messages and drafts between sides that won't negotiate directly.
keyTerms.example: Qatar shuttles drafts between Washington and Tehran.

keyTerms.definition: A hopeful sign that fades without a real change. Oil traders use it for peace-talk rallies that reverse.

watchNext.what: Any draft agreement from the Qatar-led talks, and Trump's next comments on strikes.

stories.headline: October CPI rises 0.4%, hotter than expected, with core up 0.3% for a third straight month
stories.dek: The hot print keeps a December hike near-certain and puts a 50bp move on the table after Fed Governor Waller's marker; BLS has no year-over-year figure because of last year's shutdown gap.
tldr: Headline CPI rose **0.4%** in October vs. about **0.3%** expected (forecasts ran 0.2%–0.3%); **core rose 0.3%** (unrounded about 0.297%) vs. 0.2% expected, the third straight 0.3%.
Gasoline rose 1% after September's 9.1% jump; recreation, medical care, car insurance and airline fares pushed core higher.
BLS has **no year-over-year figure** for October (no prices were collected in October 2025 during the shutdown); an Axios estimate puts it near 4%, or 2.8% excluding food and energy.
whatHappened: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that consumer prices rose 0.4% in October, above the 0.3% consensus. [[core CPI|Core CPI]], which excludes food and energy, rose 0.3% against an expected 0.2%, the third straight month at that pace (the unrounded figure was about 0.297%). Gasoline rose 1%, a sharp slowdown from September's 9.1%, but recreation, medical care, car insurance and airline fares lifted core, and food and rent costs also rose.

One quirk: BLS did not collect prices in October 2025 because of the government shutdown, so there is no official year-over-year rate for October. Axios estimated, assuming October 2025 prices were halfway between September and November, that annual inflation is about 4%, or 2.8% excluding food and energy. That is an estimate, not a BLS number.

Why markets cared: Fed Governor Christopher Waller had said a 50-[[basis-point|basis points]] hike should be considered at the December meeting if core CPI rose 0.3% or more, and reports note he still backed at least a 25bp hike either way. The print landed right on his marker. Estimates of a [[50bp December move|supersized hike]] jumped from about 1% to roughly 10%–14% depending on the source, while a 25bp hike became close to fully priced, and Treasury yields rose sharply (see below).
background: Inflation had been running hot on the energy shock, and the Fed hiked in September and held at 3.75%–4.00% on Oct. 28 with two officials dissenting for a hike. This was the last CPI before the Dec. 8–9 meeting, which is why a 0.3% core print carries so much weight: it is the third straight month, and it ends the hope that oil's slide would take the pressure off quickly.
whyItMatters: The curve repriced up: the 2-year, which tracks the expected policy path, moved the most, and the 10-year closed back above 5%. A bigger hike would pressure long-duration assets such as tech, which fits with Nvidia's drop. The counterweight is oil, down sharply over two weeks, which should show up in November's gasoline number.

grandLine.title: Akainu's Absolute Justice
grandLine.body: Akainu accepts heavy collateral damage to stamp out any trace of the threat. A Fed weighing a 50bp hike into an energy shock has the same logic: inflation is the enemy, and overtightening is the collateral damage. Waller's 0.3% marker is the Admiral's trigger, and the print hit it.

views.thesis: Three straight 0.3% core prints justify a 50bp December move.
views.argument: Core has stayed at 0.3% for three months, the labor market is strong (payrolls +165,000), and Waller has already named 50bp as the response to exactly this print.
views.who: Fed Governor Christopher Waller, per reports of his remarks.

views.thesis: A quarter-point is enough while oil falls.
views.argument: Gasoline slowed to +1% in October, Brent is down sharply from its peak, and even Waller backed only 25bp as a floor. A 50bp move risks overtightening into a supply shock.

interview.question: CPI came in at 0.4% headline and 0.3% core, above expectations. What do you do?
interview.answer: The 25bp December hike is close to fully priced, so the question is 50bp. Core at 0.3% for a third month and Waller's marker make a bigger hike live, and the 2-year yield moved the most, up 14 to 19bp. My view is to be short the front end into the December meeting but size small, since oil is falling and a lot is priced. What changes my mind is a soft November core or a sharp further drop in oil.

followUp.question: Why is there no year-over-year number?
followUp.answer: BLS didn't collect October 2025 prices during the shutdown, so there's no clean base for comparison; analysts like Axios estimate around 4%.

keyTerms.definition: Consumer prices excluding food and energy; a cleaner read on underlying inflation.
One hundredth of a percentage point. A 50bp hike is a half-point move, double the usual 25bp.
A rate increase larger than the standard 25 basis points, usually 50bp, used to move faster against inflation.

stories.headline: Stocks slip after hot CPI as the 10-year yield tops 5% and Nvidia falls nearly 5%
stories.dek: The Dow fell 0.3% and the S&P 500 0.4% a day after a 2.3% rally, with the Nasdaq down about 0.7%; Treasury yields rose sharply on bets for a bigger Fed hike.
tldr: Tuesday close: **Dow -0.30% to 52,233.32**, **S&P 500 -0.38% to 7,521.11**, **Nasdaq about -0.7%**; some outlets show slightly smaller declines.
The **10-year yield rose to about 5.0%** and the 2-year jumped 14–19bp after hot CPI put a 50bp December hike in play.
Nvidia fell about **5%** at the close, for a second straight day of heavy selling.
whatHappened: Stocks gave back part of Monday's rally after the October CPI came in hotter than expected. At the close, Investing.com had the Dow down 0.30% at 52,233.32 and the S&P 500 down 0.38% at 7,521.11, and the Nasdaq Composite fell about 0.7% (Yahoo Finance and Investing.com); a 24/7 Wall St. close showed somewhat smaller declines, so treat the percentages as approximate. Nvidia fell about 5% by the close, weighing on tech (it also slid premarket Monday after Dow Jones reported the company launched an investigation tied to reports about CEO Jensen Huang; the New York Times had reported that US intelligence tied a Megaspeed executive close to Huang to Beijing, which Nvidia disputes), and energy held up best among sectors while utilities and materials lagged.

Rates moved more than stocks: the 10-year Treasury yield rose about 15bp to roughly 5.0% and the 2-year rose 14 to 19bp depending on the source, as traders added bets that the Fed could hike by 50bp in December. I could not verify Tuesday's oil settle or the dollar.
background: Monday's rally was fueled by oil falling on Iran-diplomacy hopes; Tuesday's CPI reminded markets that core inflation hasn't cooled. The S&P 500 was still about 3.7% below its Oct. 6 high after the drop.
whyItMatters: When yields rise toward 5%, long-[[duration]] assets such as tech get repriced because future earnings are discounted at a higher [[discount rate]]. That is the link between a CPI beat and an AI-stock selloff, and it is why the same macro data can hit Nasdaq harder than the Dow.

grandLine.title: Aokiji's Lazy Justice vs. Akainu
grandLine.body: After a week of hoping the Fed could be Aokiji and wait, the CPI print handed the argument back to Akainu. The market has to price the hawk winning the fight over who runs the institution.

views.thesis: Higher yields drive the selloff in tech.
views.argument: With the 10-year at 5% and a 50bp hike on the table, the discount rate rises and long-duration stocks like Nvidia fall most.

views.thesis: A small pullback after a 2.3% rally is normal.
views.argument: The Dow and S&P fell only about 0.3% to 0.4% after the biggest rebound in months, which looks like consolidation rather than a new leg down.

interview.question: Stocks fell less than 0.5% on a hot CPI. Why were yields the bigger story?
interview.answer: Because the surprise was about the policy path, and rates absorb it first. The 2-year moved 14 to 19bp and the 10-year topped 5%. Equities were cushioned by Monday's momentum and lower oil, but tech fell more since higher yields hit duration. I'd watch the 10-year at 5% as a line in the sand. What changes my mind is a quick fall in yields or oil.

followUp.question: Why does the 10-year at 5% matter?
followUp.answer: It's a round-number level that competes with equity yields and is near the highest in years, so crossing it tends to trigger repositioning.

keyTerms.definition: How sensitive an asset's value is to changes in interest rates; long-duration assets such as growth stocks and long bonds fall most when yields rise.
keyTerms.example: Nvidia and the Nasdaq lagged as the 10-year reached 5%.

keyTerms.definition: The interest rate used to value future cash flows; higher rates lower the present value of future earnings.

watchNext.what: US bond market closed; stocks trade, so liquidity in rates is thin.

stories.headline: Nasdaq jumps 1.6% to erase its post-election losses as CoreWeave beats and Apple hits a record
stories.dek: The S&P 500 gained 1.3% to 7,619.38 and the Dow 0.5% on a day the bond market was closed for Veterans Day.
tldr: Tech led after **CoreWeave** beat on earnings; **Apple** hit a record high; Nvidia snapped a two-day slide despite a downgrade.
The S&P 500 is within about **2.6%** of its all-time high. The US bond market was closed, so Treasury yields didn't trade.
whatHappened: Stocks rallied Wednesday, led by AI and chip names. The S&P 500 rose 98.45 points, or 1.31%, to 7,619.38, the Nasdaq Composite gained 400.31 points, or 1.60%, to 25,466.19, and the Dow added 254.60 points, or 0.49%, to 52,486.49, per CappNotes' closing figures; other recaps show slightly different levels (24/7 Wall St. had the Nasdaq up about 1.55%). Yahoo Finance said the Nasdaq's gain erased its post-election losses. CoreWeave's earnings beat helped AI-infrastructure names, TheStreet reported Apple hit a new record high, and Nvidia snapped a two-day slide despite a Wall Street downgrade. Stocks were open for Veterans Day while the bond market was closed, so there was no read on Treasury yields after Tuesday's 5% 10-year. I could not verify the oil settle.
background: The Nasdaq entered a [[correction]] last Thursday, bounced, then fell again after Tuesday's hot CPI. Wednesday's jump brings the S&P 500 back within about 2.6% of its high, but that came on a day when rates didn't trade, so the test of the yield story is Thursday.
whyItMatters: Equities shrugged off a 5% 10-year with the bond market shut. When Treasuries reopen, a catch-up move in yields (a higher [[discount rate]]) could reprice the rally, which is why a holiday-session rally with no rates trading deserves skepticism.

grandLine.title: Gear 5
grandLine.body: Luffy's Gear 5 turns the rules of physics into a cartoon where anything bounces back. A one-day rebound that erases a week of losses can feel like that, but it only becomes a real recovery if the rules, here the discount rate, stay on your side.

views.thesis: AI earnings are still strong enough to carry the market.
views.argument: CoreWeave beat, Apple hit a record and the Nasdaq erased its post-election losses, so the AI trade has momentum.

views.thesis: A rally with the bond market shut is suspect.
views.argument: Rates were closed, a 5% 10-year and a possible 50bp hike are unresolved, and holiday sessions are thin.

interview.question: The Nasdaq erased its losses on a day the bond market was shut. Do you trust it?
interview.answer: Partly. The earnings were real, but a holiday session lacks the rates information that drove Tuesday. I'd wait for Thursday's bond reopening: if the 10-year stays near 5% and stocks hold, that's a stronger signal. What changes my mind is a yield spike that knocks tech lower.

followUp.question: Why does a bond-market holiday matter for stocks?
followUp.answer: Treasury yields set the discount rate; without them trading, one of the main inputs to equity valuation is frozen.

keyTerms.definition: A decline of 10% or more from a recent peak.
The interest rate used to value future cash flows; higher rates cut the present value of future earnings.

watchNext.what: Bond market reopens; does the 10-year hold near 5% and do stocks hold their gains?

stories.headline: Iran says Hormuz stays shut until seven conditions are met, even as Qatar reports progress
stories.dek: Iran's security chief denied talks with Washington while the US moved to extend its naval blockade; oil had fallen about 5% on Monday on diplomacy hopes (no newer price confirmed).
tldr: Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, said Tehran holds **no negotiations** with the US and Hormuz stays closed until **seven conditions** are met.
Reports say Iran would resume talks in as little as two days if the US halts attacks, lifts its port blockade and waives some sanctions.
Qatar says it sees progress; the US is pushing a task force to extend the blockade, which Iran's military called 'wordplay.' Brent was roughly $93–97 on Monday.
whatHappened: Iran's public line hardened this week. Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei said Tehran is holding no negotiations with the United States and that the Strait of Hormuz will remain closed until Washington meets all seven Iranian conditions. A separate report says Iran's proposal would resume talks in as little as two days if the US halted attacks, lifted its blockade of Iranian ports and waived some sanctions. Qatar, the main mediator, says it sees progress after a White House meeting, and Trump spoke with Qatar's emir. Meanwhile the US is pushing a military task force to extend its naval blockade, which Iran's military dismissed as 'wordplay.' No agreement has been announced.

For oil: Brent fell about 5% to roughly $93–97 on Monday on diplomacy hopes after a roughly 16% weekly drop, and I could not find a confirmed price for Tuesday or Wednesday. Because Hormuz flows are still far below normal, the [[risk premium]] that has drained could rebuild quickly if talks are publicly denied.
background: Hormuz is the [[chokepoint]] for about a quarter of seaborne oil. The war started Feb. 28; a June memorandum collapsed in July, and the US reimposed a blockade on Iranian ports. Iran uses control of the strait as leverage for sanctions relief.
whyItMatters: Oil trades on whether the strait reopens. A public denial from Iran's security chief is a reminder that the market's roughly 16% drop is priced on hope, and a breakdown could reverse it.

grandLine.title: Crossing the Red Line
grandLine.body: There are only two ways to cross the Red Line: through Mary Geoise with permission, or under the sea via Fish-Man Island. Whoever controls the passages controls trade between the seas. Hormuz is the oil world's Red Line, and Iran is telling the world the gate stays shut until its conditions are met.

views.thesis: Public denials are bargaining, and a deal is still coming.
views.argument: Qatar reports progress, Iran has outlined a path to resume talks in two days, and Trump keeps calling strikes unlikely if a deal is strong.

views.thesis: The sides are far apart and the premium returns.
views.argument: Iran denies talking, the US is extending its blockade, and Rubio said Iran's demands are outrageous.

interview.question: Iran says no talks and Hormuz stays shut. Why isn't oil spiking?
interview.answer: Because markets weigh action over rhetoric, and Qatar, Pakistan and others report progress. But the price is built on hope, so I'd keep the position light. What changes my mind is a signed memorandum, which is bearish oil, or renewed attacks on shipping, which is bullish.

followUp.question: What is the blockade?
followUp.answer: A US naval blockade of Iranian ports used to pressure Tehran; Iran wants it lifted in exchange for reopening Hormuz.

keyTerms.definition: A narrow passage that a large share of global trade must go through, such as Hormuz.
Extra price for uncertainty over supply or policy; it shrinks on peace hopes.

watchNext.what: Any Qatar-announced draft, and whether Iran or the US moves first on the blockade.

trade.expression: Buy a near-dated Brent call spread (e.g., 100/110), small size
trade.rationale: Oil has fallen on hope while Hormuz flows are still far below normal. A call spread caps the cost and pays if talks collapse or attacks resume. Interview framing, not advice.
risks: A signed deal reopens the strait and oil keeps falling.
Options decay if headlines stay noisy but prices don't move.
